blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we step into a sunny garden.
First, meet a little girl who grew a sunflower taller than a bus.
Then, discover the secret: do sunflowers really follow the sun all day?
Ready?
Let's go!
In a small English town lives a five-year-old girl named Lucy.
She joined a sunflower growing competition for children.
She did not need anything expensive: just pots, compost and sunshine.
Her approach was simple: she planted seeds in pots at the front of the house, where there was plenty of sunshine, and protected the shoots with old water bottles cut in half.
It was not easy: she lost one plant, another fell over, and the wind blew the top off a third!
But one plant kept growing and growing.
Soon it was taller than her dad.
At that altitude, Dad had to climb onto the car roof just to tie the plant to its canes!
First one cane, then a longer one, then three canes tied together.
Guess how tall it grew?
4.48 metres — taller than a double-decker bus!
Lucy won the competition, and everyone celebrated her giant flower.
And it did not cost much at all: just seeds, sunshine and patience.
When the flower opened, sparrows came hoping for the precious seeds.
Lucy showed us that even small hands can grow something huge.
Now: do sunflowers really follow the sun?
The answer is yes — but only when they are young!
A young sunflower turns its face from east in the morning to west in the evening, just as you turn your forehead toward the warm morning sun.
At night, it quietly turns back to the east, ready for sunrise.
How does it move?
It does not spin like a machine.
The secret is in the stem: water and liquid food travel up inside the stem, and the tissue on the shaded side grows faster, so the stem bends slowly toward the light.
Scientists call this daily dance heliotropism: a slow, steady pulse, like the plant's own inner clock.
But the most surprising aspect: when the flower grows up, it stops dancing!
A mature sunflower stays facing east all day.
Why?
An east-facing flower warms up fast in the morning, and warm flowers attract more bees.
Scientists conducted an experiment: they turned some flowers to face west, and the east-facing flowers attracted five times as many pollinators!
So the sunflower's trick is not just following the sun — it is knowing when to stop.
Today's idiom is "a wild goose chase." It means a search for something you will probably never find.
For example: looking for one tiny seed in a huge field is a wild goose chase!
And hunting for Lucy's lost water bottle all over the garden?
That would be a wild goose chase too!
But growing a sunflower is not a wild goose chase: with sunshine, water and patience, you will really see it grow.
Try it this week: tell your family about a wild goose chase you once had!
Now it is your turn!
Two questions for you.
One: Lucy's sunflower grew 4.48 metres tall.
Can you find something near your home about that tall?
Two: a young sunflower follows the sun, but a grown-up one faces east.
Why do you think facing east helps the flower?
Talk about it with your family!
That is all for today, young explorers.
We appreciate you listening and learning with us.
Keep your eyes open, keep asking questions, and we will meet tomorrow morning.
Goodbye, and have a wonderful day!
